name: Shared layers stay closed to specifics
when: Changes to integration layers, connectors, coordinators, dispatchers, registries, base classes and shared interfaces. Also driver modules that build or consume another module's descriptors, plans or specs.
expect: Move each specific behavior and its docs into its own module behind one generic extension point: a dispatcher created once at init and called once per hook, self-registration or package discovery selected by key, or the existing device/platform backend interface. Move construction and derivation of a structure into its owning module, which exposes a minimal API (one build and one consume entry point) and keeps internals private. Move non-inherent capabilities off base types into an opt-in protocol or mixin that callers depend on. The author confirms that adding a new variant or field touches no existing shared or driver file. Check: List the existing files that would have to change if (a) a second feature, implementation or vendor of this kind were added or removed next month, or (b) a new field or parameter were added to the structure this code builds or consumes. If the list includes the shared or driver module, flag it. Also flag shared or driver code that imports, names, looks up, branches on, special-cases, documents or builds the internals of a specific variant or of another module's structure. For any capability placed on a base type, ask whether it is inherent to what that base type represents, or only needed by today's subclasses.
why: Generic, shared or orchestrating code must not know about specific features, implementations, vendors, or the internals of structures owned by another module. Variants and new fields can then be added, removed or plugged in without editing it.

name: One owner, one path
when: Storing references to engine-owned or other components' objects. In-place writes into memory others may share. Cross-submodule calls inside the MP engine. New APIs, endpoints, snapshot calls or handlers that move state between components.
why: Every resource, reference and piece of propagated state has exactly one owner. That owner controls the lifetime, the writes and the propagation mechanism. Everyone else reaches it through that owner or through the single existing pipeline.

name: Bounded worst case on contended resources
when: GPU-side temporaries whose size scales with request or data length. Handlers or work placed on single-threaded or shared execution lanes, including liveness and health paths.
expect: Report the worst-case footprint. If it is unbounded or large, chunk the work with a fixed byte cap that preserves the unchunked version's ordering guarantees across chunk boundaries, and add a test that chunked output equals unchunked output. Move potentially blocking work off the single shared thread. Keep liveness probes off any lane that can block. Check: State the peak extra device memory, or the longest time it can hold the thread, for the longest realistic request or the slowest dependency (I/O, locks, registration, waiting on another component). Name the other work that shares that resource and would fail or stall meanwhile. If the cost cannot be stated, or grows without a cap, flag it.
why: Work that runs on a resource that other work shares and that may already be saturated, such as nearly full device memory or a single dispatcher thread, must have a bounded worst-case footprint. Otherwise it can OOM or stall everything else.
examples: team-v1-001: a GPU-side operation that can run while device memory or the KV pool is nearly full allocates temporaries whose size scales with the request or data size

name: Boundary contracts hold for every counterpart
when: Calling new APIs on components that have fallbacks. Reconnection and recovery paths. GPU event creation for transfers. LMCache-side workarounds for engine behavior.
why: Code that interacts across a process, version or project boundary must state the counterpart's contract explicitly. That contract must hold for every counterpart and context the code can meet at runtime, not just the common one.
examples: team-v1-003: a change alters LMCache behavior to compensate for how an upstream engine reports or handles state
team-v1-005: a reconnection or recovery path restores a connection to a peer that negotiated parameters during the initial handshake
m4736-001: a change creates, records, passes or waits on a GPU synchronization event for a KV transfer between LMCache and the serving engine, or merges event creation for
m4736-002: code that can fall back at runtime to another copy or version of a component it depends on (a vendored, bundled, older or third-party implementation) is changed
